title: Zamjenice
theme: Mene versus me shows the long form after a little word like kod.
reviewerNotes: Fresh pedagogy polish after Fact Checker. Little-word language standardized; look gloss fragment expanded; pattern opener softened. Bosnian pronoun forms retained (mene/me, tebe/te, njega/je, kod mene, za mene). Status draft; reviewedAt null. Pending human publish decision. whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn why Bosnian has a long me and a short me, and why a little word like kod forces the long one. English already splits I and me. Bosnian splits me again into mene and me. Book 1 already gave you Amira saying kahvu kod mene. That long form after kod is the whole point today.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because it only keeps one me after I. You say she sees me and coffee at my place without a second outfit for me. Bosnian keeps a full form and a short form for the same job. The short form leans on the doing-word, like me in Vidi me. The full form stands on its own, like mene when you need stress or when a little word such as kod sits in front. Schools call these words zamjenice, which means pronouns. You can keep saying long me and short me and still be right.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you Amira’s line Danas pijemo kahvu kod mene, which means today we drink coffee at my place. Kod is a little word that sits in front of the person. After that little word Bosnian needs the long form mene, not the short me. Today you contrast that line with short me after a doing-word, and you keep the same coffee on the table.
knownLine.speaker: Amira
knownLine.english: Today we drink coffee at my place!

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: You use short me when it can lean on the doing-word, and long mene when it must stand alone or follow a little word in front. Vidi me means see me, and the short form rides behind the doing-word. Kod mene means at my place, and the long form follows kod. The same split shows up on you as te versus tebe, and on him as ga versus njega. Ja versus mene or me is only a light pointer back to name-it versus want-it, not a second case lesson. Learn ja, mene, and me first on the coffee lines, then copy the same long-versus-short habit onto ti.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Two pests will trip you today. The first pest is saying kod me, which tries to hang the short form after a little word that needs the long one. The second pest is saying Vidi mene every time, which is not always wrong for stress, but it sounds heavy when short me is the everyday lean. Book 1 also gave you Boli me glava for a short me that leans on the doing-word. Keep kod mene for the little-word line, and keep me for the lean.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to treat mene and me as two different people. They are the same me in two outfits. The other trap is to borrow English at me and say na me or kod me. After a little word in front, Bosnian wants the long outfit. Short me has nowhere sturdy to lean if the only neighbor is kod or za. That is why Amira says kod mene when the coffee is at her place.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester already split I and me for the job in the sentence. You still own that split. Later English mostly stopped making a second, lighter me that could lean on the doing-word.

Bosnian kept both a full form and a lean form. The short ones are little words that prefer second place in the sentence, which Chapter 12 will unpack. Today you only need the coffee-table rule. If a little word is already sitting in front, grab mene. If the doing-word can carry the lean, me is enough.

items.prompt: Coffee at my place. Which form after kod?
items.explanation: A little word in front needs the long form. Kod mene.

items.prompt: Someone says kod me. What went wrong?
options: They used the short form after a little word

items.prompt: I want coffee. Which form does the wanting?
items.explanation: Ja is the name-it form. Mene and me are the ones that get hit.

Yes. Mene is a different person from me.

questions.question: The beer is for him. Which form after za?
questions.explanation: Za needs the long form. Za njega. Short ga leans on a doing-word like Vidim ga.

questions.question: Danas pijemo kahvu kod mene. Why mene?

questions.explanation: A little word in front leaves short me nowhere to lean.

questions.question: Vidi me uses which outfit?
options: Short form leaning on the doing-word

questions.question: Which is wrong?
questions.explanation: Kod me is the pest. Use kod mene.

questions.question: Ja želim kahvu. What is ja doing?
options: Doing the wanting in the name-it form
questions.explanation: Ja does the thing. Mene and me get hit.

options: Matching my to coffee again as the only topic
Present tense for real on doing-words
questions.explanation: Part 3 starts with Chapter 8, present tense.

next.body: You now know why mene and me are the same me in two outfits, and why kod mene needs the long form. Short forms lean on the doing-word. Chapter 8 starts the doing-word map for real, the present tense behind the Book 1 chunks. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
